title: Org Structure (Departments & People)
markdown:
The org model has two persistent registries backed by SQLite (both share `episodic_memory.db`): **departments** and **people**. Eight default departments are seeded exactly once per database on first boot, tracked by a `default_departments_seeded` sentinel in `departments_meta`; after that the user owns the list and deleted departments stay deleted across restarts.

### Company setup (onboarding)
Both registries are first populated by **conversational onboarding** at
`/onboard`. The user describes their business in their own words (optionally
attaching a deck or one-pager); the `onboarding_interviewer` agent — Council-
visible but outside `SPECIALIST_REGISTRY`, so the Executive cannot reach it via
`consult_specialist` — asks up to 8 clarifying questions, then emits a draft
company profile, a leadership roster, and a department list. The user reviews
and edits that draft inline (the same section editors `/company-profile` uses)
before anything is written.

Two properties matter here. First, **the interview never writes**: the whole
exchange lives in an in-memory, TTL'd session, and the single write happens at
`POST /onboard/interview/commit`, so a rejected save leaves the draft editable
and retryable. Second, **the department step is additive** — drafted
departments are matched onto existing ones by slug or title and updated in
place, unmatched ones are created, and nothing is ever deleted. That is
deliberately unlike the fixture loader's `_seed_departments`, which DELETEs
every row first: doing that here would drop the eight defaults along with their
`specialist_key` wiring, which onboarding's `create_department` calls (no
`specialist_key`) cannot restore. Matching goes through
`departments.store.match_department` (slug as given or as the store would slug
it, else case-insensitive title), the same rule the `create_goal` chat tool uses. `profile.org_structure` is derived from the reviewed
people and department tables at commit time, so it cannot drift from them.

Exactly one person is marked `is_principal` and receives `WILDCARD` authority;
no contact details are imported, even if the user volunteers them, because
channels and handles are a deliberate action on the People page. The one
exception is the owner's own sign-in email: the review screen has a separate
field for it, pre-filled with the current owner's email on a re-run and with the
signed-in user's on a first setup. The commit checks it before writing anything
(malformed, already another person's, or different from the owner's existing
email is a 422 — setup only fills in a missing one) and then saves it on the
principal's row. Without it the signed-in owner matched no Person,
so their chat history stayed empty until they found the People page. With
local login (`make dev` without Google sign-in) the field is optional: that
session carries no email, which the backend already reads as the principal.
Because the save demotes the old principal, only the current owner may draft
someone else as "This is me" when setup is re-run (403 otherwise); a re-run
that keeps the owner, or a first setup, is open to anyone who can sign in. On such a re-run, someone who isn't the owner may fill in the owner's missing email only with the address they signed in with (403 otherwise): the roster is the sign-in allow-list, so any other address would let them sign in as the owner. That keeps the way in for an owner whose entry has no email, which is also where Setup status and the Executive send them, since the People page refuses anyone it can't recognise as the owner. Re-running setup stays open to everyone deliberately: the Company Profile and Departments pages already let anyone signed in change the same things. The original
12-step form wizard remains available at `/onboard?mode=form` and backs the
`openexecutive onboard` CLI. It adds people with their emails, so once there is an owner only they can save it.

A first setup opens on one question — **Just me** or **Me and my team** — and
the choice is written to `PUT /workspace` (with the browser's time zone) before
the conversation starts, because the two modes ask different things. **Just
me** then asks the principal's role (skippable, editable later in Settings):
which describes them — owner / founder, an executive inside an organisation,
independent or fractional, or other — their title, who they report to, what
they are responsible for and what they are measured on, saved to the same
workspace settings. A re-run over an existing profile skips both; they are
changed in Settings. In solo the interviewer's first user turn carries a short
hint, one static constant per role kind (`onboarding.interview.solo_hint`):
always draft only the principal, as principal, and no departments; an owner is
asked about the offer, customers, pricing, cash and runway; an in-house
executive about their organisation (the company profile is their employer),
their function and remit, their manager, their team size as context rather
than a roster, and what they are measured on; an independent about their
practice, clients and pricing; with no role given, the role-neutral hint asks
which of these they are. Each also asks their top goals. The hint never
carries the principal's own text, and it rides in the user turn, so the cached
system prompt is the same constant in both modes. The solo review screen shows only **You**
(name and role) and the sign-in email, and commits that one principal with no
departments — the existing departments stay, as the areas goals are grouped
by. The form wizard (and the CLI) read the mode when a session starts and skip
the Team Size, Team Members and Fractional Executives steps in solo; each
status response numbers the steps it actually asks and flags whether the
current one is `optional`.

### Departments
Each department carries a charter, `Goal` rows, `ChecklistItem`s, and named cadences. Cadence specs (`daily@HH:MM`, `weekly@DOW@HH:MM`, `quarterly@DD-HH:MM`, UTC) run a `department_check_in` workflow when due (never in solo mode, below), then chain the next occurrence; `PATCH /departments/{slug}` rejects a spec that does not parse with a 422. The check-in is skipped (and still chained) when the department has no specialist, no Goals, or nothing new since its Goals were last reviewed. An idle initiative is chased with the department's head, or with the principal when there is none. A department may map to a specialist agent via `specialist_key`, or stay informational. No department is seeded for the `sales` specialist (existing installs keep their departments unchanged), so its consults skip the department-memory prefetch and the Honcho department sync, as `triage`'s do. An assigned head gets a generated department-head voice persona.

**Goals from chat.** Besides the goal routes and the UI, the Executive keeps goals current from a chat turn: `update_department_goal` records reported progress, and `create_goal` starts tracking a new goal the principal states ("20 paying clients by the end of Q4"). Only the principal, on a surface that verified it is them (`people_tools.is_principal_on_verified_surface`, the roster tools' rule: the web chat, their own Slack or Discord, a private Telegram chat with a valid webhook secret), may call it: a goal renders in every turn's org block as one of the principal's own, so a goal from an inbound email, Google Chat, a teammate or an unattended run would be text carrying their authority. Anyone else gets a refusal (audited with the caller and surface) and nothing is written. `create_goal` names the area as free text — a slug or a title, resolved by `match_department` — so its schema is static and adding an area never changes the cached tool prefix. When nothing matches it creates the area (`create_department`), giving it a specialist only when the title is obviously one's domain (`specialist_key_for_area`: the default departments' slugs and titles, plus Sales) and no department holds that specialist yet; anything else is informational. It refuses a goal the area already tracks (pointing at `update_department_goal`), caps a turn at 5 new goals (a sweep is not a stated goal) and an area at 8 (common practice keeps 3–5 key results per objective, and every goal renders in the 4000-character org block, so one area cannot crowd the others out), returns only the exception type on a store failure, is audited with its rationale, and is never offered to an unattended run (`schedule_tools.UNATTENDED_WITHHELD_TOOLS`: reflection, research and the scheduler's proactive trigger). The solo persona teaches it; team mode learns it from the tool description, so the team persona stays byte-identical.

A department can also list **watched entities** (`watched_entities`, edited one per line on its page): vendors it is evaluating, competitors in its lane, tickers it tracks. The research watch policy treats them as strong grounding — a proposal about one can be added to the watch list on its own — and routes the resulting watch, its alerts and any suggestion cards to the department and its head rather than the principal (see External monitoring).

### Solo and team mode
An install is either a **team** (the default) or **solo** — one person using Open Executive just for themselves. The mode lives with the user's time zone in its own one-row table, `workspace_settings` (`openexecutive.memory.workspace_settings`, `GET`/`PUT /workspace`), not on the company profile, because onboarding's commit and the form wizard rebuild the profile from scratch and would wipe it. Changing it is the principal's call (open while no principal exists, so first-run setup can choose).

The same row holds the **principal's role** (`PrincipalRole`, every field nullable): `role_kind` (`owner`, `in_house`, `independent` or `other`), `role_title`, `reports_to` (free text, e.g. "VP of Operations, Dana Ruiz"), `remit` (what they are responsible for) and `measured_on` (what they are judged on). Solo is about who uses Open Executive, not the principal's level — a business owner, an executive inside a larger organisation, an independent or fractional executive — and this is the context the solo persona reads the role from. Only solo mode reads it; a mode switch keeps it. `GET /workspace` returns it only to the principal (nulls for anyone else). The columns are added to an existing table additively, and a read of an older table (no role columns yet) never migrates it and reads the role as unset.

Solo also changes how the Executive speaks and what it can do. It works for one person — the principal — without assuming their role (an owner, an executive inside a larger organisation, or an independent); the people in their world are contacts it helps them work with, not a team it routes to. The cached org block becomes the principal's own line ("Your Principal") — followed by their role lines when a role is set (`- Role: <title> — <kind in plain words>`, `- Reports to:`, `- Responsible for:`, `- Measured on:`, each only when set, sanitized and capped) — plus their goals grouped by **area** (a department row is an area; no authority levels, heads, cadences, channels or roster), and posting to a department room, broadcasting to the company and assigning a department head are not offered. Specialists never see that block, so each consult in a solo turn also carries a `<principal_role>` tag in its user turn (kind, title and remit, resolved once per turn with the org block's role), so a VP inside a large company is told to make the case to their CFO rather than to raise a round. A follow-up the Executive schedules to the principal goes straight to them — its department and scope are dropped, so the authority gate never files a card asking the principal to approve a message to themselves. Meeting bookings are gated on the `meeting_scheduling` class mode, not a department (see below).

Solo turns the department rhythm off without touching the org: switching to solo cancels every pending `dept_cadence` row, `bootstrap_cadences` does nothing (the check sits inside it, so boot, the fixture reset and client-slot activation all honour it), and the scheduler cancels any stray check-in without running or chaining it, and a check-in already running across the switch schedules no successor. Department and people rows are kept, so switching back to team re-schedules the check-ins at once. The boot-time org-completeness warnings (departments with no head) are skipped in solo. A chat `Session` can carry an explicit `workspace_mode` override (read through `effective_workspace_mode`), so a caller that runs many conversations on one Executive — evals, for one — can pick the mode per session instead of flipping the install-wide setting; a `principal_role` override (read through `effective_principal_role`) does the same for the role.

In the UI, a `WorkspaceProvider` in the root layout reads the mode and role once (and again after Settings changes them) and reads **team** while loading or on error, so a team install never flashes the solo UI. Solo swaps the sidebar's Company group for **You** — Goals, People, Business profile — where `/goals` lists every goal grouped by area (a department row) and adds, edits and deletes them through the slug-scoped goal routes. `/departments` and `/people` stay reachable by URL.

The setting is per company: a blank client slot starts on the defaults, a saved slot keeps its own (restoring one runs the additive column migration), a fixture load resets it and applies the fixture's optional `workspace.yaml` (`mode`, `timezone` and the optional role keys; read and validated before anything is swapped; a bad value is skipped, never a failed load), and the factory reset returns it to team with no zone and no role. The user's own settings survive a demo: the backup a fixture load takes (or reuses) always gets the live settings written to its `workspace.yaml` while the live state is the user's, and an unload from an older backup without one leaves the settings as they are. A zone that cannot be loaded is never fatal — the API answers 422, and a stored one reads as unset.

### Authority gate
Each department declares an `AuthorityLevel`, which `departments.authority.gate_action` checks whenever a department-scoped scheduled action comes due. The check-in cadence is the exception: it sends nothing itself, and each action it proposes is run through the gate and shown with its verdict in the report — so a propose-only department's check-ins actually run instead of becoming a one-shot approval card. `auto_execute` (autonomous) fires directly. `propose_only` turns the action into an approval card for an approver (`propose_via_alert`) and sends nothing, deferring the card to the approver's next availability window when they are outside it. `escalate` also sends nothing until someone approves: it raises an urgent `[ESCALATION]` card (severity high) right away, never deferred — filed unrouted when nobody holds the scope and no principal is set, since the Briefing lists every unread card — what the Departments page promises ("the specialist will not act — it forwards everything to a human"). It used to raise the card *and* dispatch, so approving the card sent the action a second time. Calendar bookings follow the same rule in team mode. In solo mode there is no operations department to consult: the booking is decided by the `meeting_scheduling` class mode — `propose` puts it on the briefing for the principal, and `auto_execute` books right away only when the principal started the turn on a surface that verified it is them (the roster-write rule: the web chat, their own Slack or Discord, or a private Telegram chat with the webhook secret set). A booking asked for in an inbound email, by a contact, or by an unattended run is proposed to the principal instead, so text someone else wrote cannot put a meeting on their calendar. The principal sets it with `GET`/`PUT /decisions/classes/meeting_scheduling` (`{"decision_class": "meeting_scheduling", "mode": "propose" | "auto_execute"}`; the PUT is principal-only and audited). The approver is chosen by `AuthorityScope` — a scheduled action's `required_scope` (e.g. `vendor_onboarding`, `spend_lt_10k`) feeds `find_approvers(scope)`, which ranks non-principal scope-holders ahead of `WILDCARD` holders. A null/unknown scope falls back to `WILDCARD` (the principal).

### People & channels
The people registry resolves each `Person` to a `(channel, channel_ref)` pair via `prefer_channel_for()`, honoring `preferred_channel` (falling back email → slack → discord → telegram) and availability windows. The principal briefs use their own order — the preferred channel, then Slack → Discord → Telegram, then email as the backup for every preference (first for an `email` one); see Scheduler. Departments can also set `slack_channel_id` / `discord_channel_id` / `telegram_chat_id` to broadcast to a team room instead of DMing the head.

Each person's page also lists their **open loops** (see Attunement) — what they committed to or were asked for in conversation — with a *Mark done* action; archiving a person closes their open loops, since an archived person can no longer be chased. The list is the principal's or that person's only; `people.store.is_principal_or_self` is the one check behind it, the close action and reply feedback.

The Executive can change the roster from a chat turn (`upsert_person`, `archive_person`, `set_department_head`) only when the principal asks, from the web chat, their own Slack or Discord, or a private Telegram chat when `TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` is set to a value Telegram can send. A teammate, an email (even one from the principal's address), Google Chat, the CLI, the MCP server and unattended runs are refused, because a People row is also the web sign-in allow-list, the outbound-email allow-list and approval routing. The People page follows the same rule: adding, editing and archiving people (`POST`/`PATCH /people`, `POST /people/{id}/archive`) are the principal's alone, or anyone's while no one is principal yet, so a first setup can add its owner (`chat._caller_is_principal_or_unclaimed`). Anyone else gets 403. That includes a teammate editing their own entry: its email and chat ids are how they sign in and how the Executive reaches them, and the rest decides their approvals and how they are chased. Their working style and open loops stay theirs. A signed-in owner whose email is on no People entry is refused too; they sign in with the email on their entry, or re-run the setup interview, which fills a missing one with the email they signed in with.
